summary: A sleep medicine for adults with insomnia (trouble falling or staying asleep) that blocks orexin, a brain signal that keeps you awake; it wears off fairly quickly, so next-day grogginess is less likely than with many sleep medicines.
description: Daridorexant is a sleep medicine for adults with insomnia, meaning trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It blocks orexin A and B, brain chemicals that keep you awake (at the OX1R and OX2R receptors). This lowers the drive to stay awake rather than slowing down the whole brain. You take it once a night (25–50 mg) within 30 minutes of bedtime, when you have at least 7 hours left for sleep. Its side effects differ from older sleep medicines that work on GABA: sleepiness or tiredness, and rare complex sleep behaviors (doing things while not fully awake). Its effect on breathing is fairly small, but there is little data in people with serious lung or breathing disease. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US (not controlled in Canada).
patient_summary: Daridorexant (Quviviq) is a prescription sleep medicine for adults who have trouble falling or staying asleep. You take it once at night, within 30 minutes of going to bed, when you can stay in bed for at least 7 hours. It works by blocking chemicals in the brain (orexins) that keep you awake. The most common side effects are feeling sleepy, tired, dizzy, or having a headache. Some people can have unusual sleep behaviors like sleepwalking or doing things while not fully awake. Don’t drink alcohol with it and don’t take it if you have narcolepsy.

primary.context: FDA/Health Canada indication for insomnia characterized by difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance in adults.

secondary.context: Use with care if you have depression now or have had it before; sleep medicines can worsen mood or bring out suicidal thoughts.
Limited data in significant respiratory disease; consider risk–benefit and monitor for respiratory compromise.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Can affect driving and how you function the next day, especially with less than 7 hours in bed, higher doses, or when taken at the same time as other medicines or substances that slow the brain.
Typically mild to moderate; often attenuates with continued use.
Contributes to fall risk in older adults; consider starting at 25 mg and counsel regarding nocturnal ambulation.

serious_risks.risk: Complex sleep behaviors: sleepwalking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls, or sexual activity while not fully awake, with amnesia for the event.
Hallucinations (hypnagogic or hypnopompic), nightmares, abnormal dreams.
Sleep paralysis (transient inability to move/speak during sleep–wake transitions).
Narcolepsy-like symptoms (eg, mild cataplexy) theoretically possible based on mechanism.
Worsening depression or emergent suicidal ideation.

contraindications.contraindication: History of hypersensitivity to daridorexant (eg, angioedema with pharyngeal involvement)
Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C; use not recommended)

precautions: Slowing of the brain: risk of impaired driving and daytime sleepiness, especially with less than 7 hours in bed, higher doses, or when taken with other medicines or substances that slow the brain (benzodiazepines, opioids, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol).
Complex sleep behaviors: Stop it for good if you have sleep-walking, sleep-driving, or other complex behaviors while not fully awake.
Sleep-related phenomena: Hallucinations, nightmares, sleep paralysis, and mild cataplexy-like episodes have been reported with orexin antagonists.
Depression / suicidality: Hypnotics can worsen mood or unmask suicidal ideation; monitor closely in MDD, bipolar disorder, and personality disorders.
Respiratory compromise: Limited data in significant COPD or other respiratory disorders; consider alternative agents or close monitoring.
Liver problems: more of the drug stays in your body with moderate liver problems, so the maximum dose is 25 mg; avoid it with severe liver problems.
Substance use risk: Schedule IV in US; risk appears lower vs GABAergic hypnotics but monitor for misuse, dose escalation, or drug-seeking behavior.
Appropriate use: Persistent insomnia beyond 7–10 days may indicate underlying psychiatric or medical illness that requires further diagnostic workup.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that strongly slow its breakdown (CYP3A4 inhibitors), e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, some boosted HIV regimens
interactions.mechanism: These medicines slow how your body breaks down daridorexant, so levels rise a lot and you are more likely to get too sleepy or have other side effects.
interactions.action: Do not take them together; your prescriber can choose a different sleep medicine or adjust the other medicine.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that moderately slow its breakdown (CYP3A4 inhibitors), e.g., diltiazem, verapamil, erythromycin, fluconazole, grapefruit juice
interactions.action: Consider reducing daridorexant dose (eg, 25 mg max) and monitor for sedation; avoid grapefruit juice near dosing.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that speed up its breakdown (CYP3A4 inducers), e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John’s wort
interactions.mechanism: These speed up how your body breaks down daridorexant, so levels drop and it may not work as well.
interactions.action: Avoid strong inducers, or watch whether it stops working as well; your prescriber may suggest a different sleep medicine.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids, sedating antidepressants, antipsychotics, gabapentinoids, alcohol)
interactions.mechanism: Additive or synergistic CNS depression, increasing risk of sedation, falls, and respiratory events.
interactions.action: Use the lowest doses that work for all of them; where possible, use just one medicine for sleep; avoid alcohol.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that rely on the same breakdown and transport pathways (CYP3A4 or P-gp)
interactions.mechanism: Daridorexant slightly slows the breakdown of some other medicines (CYP3A4 and P-gp pathways), so their levels may rise a little.
interactions.action: Typically no adjustment required, but be aware in narrow therapeutic index drugs and monitor as clinically indicated.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Clinical sleep outcomes: Sleep onset latency, total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, and daytime functioning (ideally via sleep diary).
Daytime sedation and driving ability, especially during first weeks and after dose changes.
Complex sleep behaviors: Ask routinely about sleepwalking, nocturnal eating, sleep-driving, and other unusual behaviors with amnesia.
Mood and suicidality: Screen for depressive symptoms and SI at baseline and periodically (eg, PHQ-9, C-SSRS).
Falls and balance: Particularly in older adults and those on multiple CNS depressants.
Liver blood tests: at the start and when needed, especially if you have liver problems or take many medicines.
Breathing: checked when needed if you have COPD, sleep apnea (OSA), obesity-related breathing problems, or take other medicines that slow breathing.
Adherence and misuse: Refill patterns, PDMP, and reports of dose escalation or recreational use.

special_populations.pregnancy: Animal studies do not suggest a major risk of harming a developing baby at doses several times higher than human exposure, but human data are limited. Use only if the possible benefit is worth the possible risk. A pregnancy registry is available.
special_populations.lactation: Daridorexant and metabolites are present in breast milk at low relative infant dose (~0.22% of maternal dose). Clinical impact is unknown; if used during lactation, monitor infant for excessive sedation and feeding difficulties.
special_populations.pediatric: Not indicated and not studied in people <18 years.
special_populations.geriatric: Doses are similar to younger adults, but older adults are more likely to have sleepiness, tiredness and falls. Starting at 25 mg and a careful check of fall risk are worth considering.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No adjustment in Child-Pugh A; max 25 mg in Child-Pugh B; avoid in Child-Pugh C.

pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High-fat/high-calorie meals delay Tmax and may delay sleep onset

dosing.titration: Dose selection is based on insomnia phenotype, age/comorbidity, and hepatic function. Use a single nightly dose only and ensure ≥7 hours available for sleep.

sections.heading: Clinical Indications
sections.text: Daridorexant is approved for adults with insomnia, meaning trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It is especially relevant when (1) CBT-i (cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia) is unavailable, not enough, or not wanted; (2) GABAergic hypnotics are undesirable (for example, because of fall risk, breathing risk, or effects on thinking); or (3) an orexin-based approach is preferred to avoid broadly slowing down brain activity.
items: Insomnia with sleep maintenance difficulty (middle or late-night awakenings)
Chronic insomnia when nonpharmacologic interventions have been insufficient and risks/benefits of long-term pharmacotherapy have been carefully considered

sections.heading: Position in Treatment Algorithm (Psychiatry/Sleep)
sections.text:
Daridorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA), a sleep medicine that does not work through GABA.

Compared with benzodiazepines and Z-drugs:
- It does not act directly on GABA-A; in theory this means lower risks of tolerance, rebound insomnia and dependence, though it is still a Schedule IV medication in the US.
- It slows breathing less, but caution is still needed with significant breathing or lung disease.
- It is less likely to cause next-day grogginess than medicines with longer half-lives, but impaired driving and daytime sleepiness still happen.

Compared with other DORAs (such as suvorexant and lemborexant), daridorexant has a shorter half-life (about 8 hours), and its studies focused more on daytime functioning. CBT-i is still the treatment usually tried first, with daridorexant added when non-drug approaches are not enough.

sections.heading: Dosing (Adults, 18+)
sections.text: Dose selection is based on insomnia phenotype, age/comorbidity, and hepatic function. Use a single nightly dose only and ensure ≥7 hours available for sleep.

adult.insomnia_initial: 25 mg PO once nightly within 30 minutes of bedtime when ≥7 hours remain before planned awakening.
adult.insomnia_titration: If 25 mg is well-tolerated but inadequate, may increase to 50 mg PO QHS.
adult.timing: Administer within 30 minutes of bedtime, not earlier in the evening.
adult.with_food: May be taken with or without food, but high-fat/high-calorie meals can delay onset.
adult.elderly: Same dose range (25–50 mg QHS) as younger adults; consider starting at 25 mg in frail or high fall-risk patients.
adult.hepatic_mild: Child-Pugh A: No dose adjustment required.
adult.hepatic_severe: Child-Pugh C: Use not recommended (no data).
adult.renal: No dosage adjustment in kidney impairment.
adult.canada_labeling: 50 mg once nightly within 30 minutes of bedtime (at least 7 hours before waking); some people may need 25 mg once nightly.

sections.simple_explanation: For most adults, start 25 mg once at bedtime and increase to 50 mg if needed and tolerated. Always ensure at least 7 hours in bed and avoid taking more than one dose per night.

sections.heading: Onset & Duration
sections.text: Daridorexant has a relatively quick onset and an intermediate half-life, designed to aid both sleep onset and maintenance while limiting next-day residual effects.
key_points: Onset of sleep: ~30–40 minutes after dosing.

Functional implication: Adequate to cover nocturnal sleep period if ≥7 hours in bed, but can still produce next-day sedation, particularly at 50 mg, with shorter sleep times, or when combined with CNS depressants.

sections.heading: Adverse Effects & Safety Profile
sections.summary: Generally well tolerated; most common AEs are somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, and headache. Rare but clinically significant events include complex sleep behaviors, hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and allergic reactions.
plain_language_list: Rare: complex sleep behaviors (eg, sleepwalking, sleep-driving)

common.patient_note: Can impair driving and next-day performance, especially with <7 hours in bed, higher doses, or concomitant CNS depressants.
Typically mild to moderate; often attenuates with continued use.
Contributes to fall risk in older adults; consider starting at 25 mg and counsel regarding nocturnal ambulation.

serious: Complex sleep behaviors: sleepwalking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls, or sexual activity while not fully awake, with amnesia for the event.
Hallucinations (hypnagogic or hypnopompic), nightmares, abnormal dreams.
Sleep paralysis (transient inability to move/speak during sleep–wake transitions).
Narcolepsy-like symptoms (eg, mild cataplexy) theoretically possible based on mechanism.
Worsening depression or emergent suicidal ideation.

sections.heading: Key Warnings & Precautions for Psychiatrists
sections.highlight: Orexin blockade reduces wake drive and can cause significant next-day sedation and rare narcolepsy-like phenomena. Evaluate underlying causes of insomnia before prescribing.
other: CNS depression: Risk of driving impairment and daytime somnolence, particularly with less than 7 hours in bed, higher doses, or co-administration with CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, TCAs, alcohol).
Complex sleep behaviors: Discontinue permanently if patient experiences sleep-walking, sleep-driving, or other complex behaviors while not fully awake.
Sleep-related phenomena: Hallucinations, nightmares, sleep paralysis, and mild cataplexy-like episodes have been reported with orexin antagonists.
Depression / suicidality: Hypnotics can worsen mood or unmask suicidal ideation; monitor closely in MDD, bipolar disorder, and personality disorders.
Respiratory compromise: Limited data in significant COPD or other respiratory disorders; consider alternative agents or close monitoring.
Hepatic impairment: Increased exposure in moderate hepatic dysfunction; max dose 25 mg; avoid in severe hepatic impairment.
Substance use risk: Schedule IV in US; risk appears lower vs GABAergic hypnotics but monitor for misuse, dose escalation, or drug-seeking behavior.
Appropriate use: Persistent insomnia beyond 7–10 days may indicate underlying psychiatric or medical illness that requires further diagnostic workup.
patient_counseling: Take only once per night, right before bed, when you can stay in bed ≥7 hours.
Do not drive or engage in activities that require full alertness the morning after until you know how you respond.
Avoid alcohol and combining with other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly directs otherwise.
If your sleep does not improve or your mood worsens, tell your clinician.
If others notice you doing things in your sleep (walking, eating, driving, sex) that you do not remember, stop the medication and call your clinician immediately.

sections.heading: Drug–Drug Interactions (Psychiatry-Relevant)

items.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, some boosted HIV regimens)
items.risk: Significant increase in daridorexant exposure with increased risk of excessive sedation and adverse effects.
items.action: Avoid co-administration; choose an alternative hypnotic or adjust the interacting agent.

items.with: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, diltiazem, verapamil, erythromycin, fluconazole, grapefruit juice)
items.action: Consider reducing daridorexant dose (eg, 25 mg max) and monitor for sedation; avoid grapefruit juice near dosing.

items.with: CYP3A4 inducers (eg, rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John’s wort)
items.action: Avoid strong inducers or monitor for reduced efficacy; consider alternative hypnotic.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids, sedating antidepressants, antipsychotics, gabapentinoids, alcohol)
items.risk: Additive or synergistic CNS depression, increasing risk of sedation, falls, and respiratory events.
items.action: Use lowest effective doses for all agents; consider monotherapy for insomnia where possible; counsel on avoiding alcohol.

items.with: Drugs cleared via CYP3A4 or P-gp
items.risk: Daridorexant is a weak CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitor; modest increases in exposure to sensitive substrates possible.
items.action: Typically no adjustment required, but be aware in narrow therapeutic index drugs and monitor as clinically indicated.

sections.intro: Daridorexant is primarily a CYP3A4 substrate and a weak CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitor. Dose adjustments or avoidance are required with strong/moderate CYP3A4 modulators.

sections.heading: Special Populations & Psychiatric Considerations
sections.text: Daridorexant has been studied primarily in middle-aged and older adults with primary insomnia; extrapolation to comorbid psychiatric populations is reasonable but data are still emerging.
sections.pregnancy: Animal data do not suggest major teratogenicity at multiples of human exposure, but human data are limited. Use only if potential benefit justifies the potential risk. A pregnancy registry is available.
sections.lactation: Daridorexant and metabolites are present in breast milk at low relative infant dose (~0.22% of maternal dose). Clinical impact is unknown; if used during lactation, monitor infant for excessive sedation and feeding difficulties.
sections.pediatrics: Not indicated and not studied in patients <18 years.
sections.geriatrics: Similar dosing to younger adults, but greater susceptibility to somnolence, fatigue, and falls. Consider starting at 25 mg and careful fall-risk assessment.
sections.hepatic: No adjustment in Child-Pugh A; max 25 mg in Child-Pugh B; avoid in Child-Pugh C.
sections.substance_use_disorder: Schedule IV; appears to have lower abuse liability compared with benzodiazepines, but monitor PDMP, early refills, and co-prescribed sedatives.

sections.heading: Monitoring & Follow-up
items: Clinical sleep outcomes: Sleep onset latency, total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, and daytime functioning (ideally via sleep diary).
Daytime sedation and driving ability, especially during first weeks and after dose changes.
Complex sleep behaviors: Ask routinely about sleepwalking, nocturnal eating, sleep-driving, and other unusual behaviors with amnesia.
Mood and suicidality: Screen for depressive symptoms and SI at baseline and periodically (eg, PHQ-9, C-SSRS).
Falls and balance: Particularly in older adults and those on multiple CNS depressants.
Liver function tests (LFTs): Baseline and as clinically indicated, especially in hepatic impairment or polypharmacy.
Breathing: checked when needed if you have COPD, sleep apnea (OSA), obesity-related breathing problems, or take other medicines that slow breathing.
Adherence and misuse: Refill patterns, PDMP, and reports of dose escalation or recreational use.

sections.heading: Formulations & Practical Details
sections.text: Daridorexant is supplied as film-coated oral tablets.
items: US: Quviviq tablets 25 mg and 50 mg (daridorexant hydrochloride).
Controlled status: Schedule IV in the US; not controlled in Canada.
Medication Guide: US prescribers must dispense an FDA-approved Medication Guide with each fill.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Daridorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA). It selectively and competitively blocks orexin A and B binding at OX1R and OX2R, reducing wake-promoting drive from the hypothalamic orexin system. Unlike benzodiazepines or Z-drugs, daridorexant does not potentiate GABA-A receptors and therefore may have a distinct profile with respect to cognitive impairment, tolerance, and respiratory depression, though clinically meaningful CNS depression can still occur.

faqs.q: How does daridorexant differ from benzodiazepines and Z-drugs?
faqs.a: Daridorexant antagonizes orexin receptors and reduces wake drive, rather than potentiating GABA-A. It is less broadly sedating and may carry lower risks of tolerance, rebound insomnia, and respiratory depression, but it is still a Schedule IV drug (US) with potential for sedation, falls, and misuse.

faqs.q: What dose should I start with in a typical psychiatric outpatient with insomnia?
faqs.a: Most adults can start at 25 mg within 30 minutes of bedtime with ≥7 hours in bed. If tolerated but insufficient, increase to 50 mg at bedtime. In older or frail people, it is reasonable to stay at 25 mg due to fall risk.

faqs.q: Can I take daridorexant if I have depression (MDD) and long-term insomnia?
faqs.a: Yes, but your mood and any suicidal thoughts should be watched closely. Insomnia that does not go away may be a sign that depression or another condition is not fully treated. Daridorexant is best added after your antidepressant treatment and CBT-i (therapy for insomnia) have been made as effective as possible.

faqs.q: What if I have sleep apnea (OSA) or COPD?
faqs.a: There is limited information, especially for moderate to severe breathing disease. If it is used, the lowest dose that works is chosen, CPAP should be used regularly if you have sleep apnea, and daytime sleepiness or breathing problems should be watched for. Avoid combining it with other strong medicines that slow breathing when possible.

faqs.q: When should I permanently discontinue daridorexant?
faqs.a: It should be stopped if you have complex sleep behaviors (for example, driving or walking around while not fully awake in ways that put you at risk), significant narcolepsy-like symptoms (such as sudden sleep or muscle weakness), worsening depression or suicidal thoughts linked to the medicine, or an allergic reaction (such as swelling of the face, lips or throat). Tell your prescriber right away if any of these happen.

faqs.q: Is tapering required when stopping daridorexant?
faqs.a: No step-by-step taper is needed, because of how it works and because it leaves your body fairly quickly. Still, if you feel very anxious about stopping, plan other ways to manage insomnia (such as CBT-i) before you stop, because insomnia may come back.
